results.proposed_modification: Integrate a triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) into the pacemaker to harvest biomechanical energy from cardiac motion for continuous battery recharging.
results.mechanistic_reasoning: The primary failure mode is battery depletion in lithium-iodine batteries, which currently require replacement every 5-8 years. A TENG can convert biomechanical energy from cardiac motion into electrical energy, enabling self-recharging of the pacemaker battery. Evidence shows that an implantable TENG can generate sufficient energy (0.495 μJ per cardiac cycle) to exceed the endocardial pacing threshold (0.377 μJ), demonstrating feasibility for sustained pacing without external power replacement. This directly addresses battery depletion by supplementing or replacing the finite lithium-iodine battery with a renewable energy source.
results.expected_effect: The pacemaker will maintain continuous pacing functionality for 10+ years without surgical replacement, as the TENG provides ongoing energy harvesting to extend or eliminate battery replacement cycles.
results.falsification_test: Implant a pacemaker with integrated TENG in a large-animal model (e.g., swine) and monitor its ability to sustain pacing over 10+ years without battery replacement. Measure the energy harvested per cardiac cycle and verify it consistently meets or exceeds the pacing threshold energy (0.377 μJ). If the device fails to maintain pacing due to insufficient energy harvesting, the modification is falsified.
results.why_different_from_baseline: The baseline uses a non-rechargeable lithium-iodine battery with a finite lifespan, while the proposed modification introduces a self-recharging mechanism via biomechanical energy harvesting, eliminating dependency on a single-use battery.

results.mechanistic_reasoning: The failure arises from a mismatch between the scaffold’s degradation rate and the tissue regeneration timeline (12–24 weeks). A biphasic scaffold with a faster-degrading phase (e.g., PGA) and a slower-degrading phase (e.g., PLGA) can align degradation with healing by: (1) providing early-stage support via the slower phase while the faster phase degrades to create space and release bioactive cues for tissue ingrowth, and (2) ensuring structural integrity is maintained until tissue maturation. results.expected_effect: The modification will produce a scaffold whose degradation rate more closely matches the 12–24 week tissue healing timeline, reducing the risk of premature structural failure or delayed tissue integration. results.falsification_test: Implant the modified biphasic PLGA/PGA scaffold and the baseline PLGA scaffold in a standardized in vivo bone defect model (e.g., rat critical-sized calvarial defect).
